title: How Can Democrats Make the Most of Their Win?
summary:
How Can Democrats Make the Most of Their Win?
jessica.blake@… Fri, 11/06/2026 - 03:00 AM

Policy experts say it’s not as simple as opposing all things Trump. Delivering on their affordability promises and passing practical bills will be key.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
In their campaigns to retake Congress, Democrats repeatedly pledged to lower living costs for Americans.

When it comes to college costs, that affordability agenda must first focus on closing a projected $17 billion shortfall in Pell grant funding before lawmakers tackle more ambitious policy ideas such as doubling the maximum need-based aid to $15,000, higher education experts said this week.

“You want to make sure that students can continue to get Pell before you’re trying to expand it,” said Alex Holt, a moderate right-leaning higher education policy expert. “It’s not necessarily giving students more money in their pocket. So, I can understand why that’s hard as a legislator from an affordability perspective. But ultimately you do need to save Pell. That’s an affordability issue.”

Protecting Pell is just one of several concrete steps that Democrats need to take in order to protect their new majorities and win the White House in 2028, Holt and others said. With that power, Democrats could then take bigger and bolder swings on higher ed policy.

But for the next two years, the more than half a dozen higher ed advocates, scholars and policy experts that Inside Higher Ed spoke with urged the Democrats to focus on crafting a unified vision for America’s colleges and using practical bipartisan legislation to carry it out.

Experts also acknowledged that students and institutions have raised concerns about major elements of the Republican’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act—like its loan limits for graduate students—and key House lawmakers have suggested repealing them entirely. But many cautioned that trying to reverse everything the Trump administration has done won’t be productive, in part because he’s still president and has welcomed the nickname “Mr. Veto.”

The midterm results showed Americans weren’t satisfied with the status quo, but changing the status quo in higher education doesn’t mean going back to what policies looked like before Trump, said Michelle Dimino, director of the education program at Third Way, a moderate left-leaning think tank.

“Voters are saying we don’t feel like the government is looking out for us and giving us a fair shot. It’s not making sure that things are affordable and that people are being held accountable when things go wrong,” Dimino said. “It’s a little bit baffling to see folks come down so firmly on the other side just because this is something that came out of the Trump administration as it currently stands.”

Democrats can, however, push back on the administration via hearings and use their control over the federal purse strings to add budgetary language that prevents Trump from canceling scientific research grants, forward funding fewer student success programs, and axing data collection contracts. Several experts hoped to see investigations and hearing about Education Secretary Linda McMahon’s efforts to dismantle her agency.

“The Trump administration, by my characterization, has stretched its authority, to put it nicely. So, empowering Congress to exercise more public oversight may have a substantial impact on the extent to which some of these like extra-legal efforts hold up and may squash them more quickly than would have been the case with Congress held by Republicans,” said Beth Akers, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank.

Need for ‘a Compelling Vision’

Before Democrats try to advance any particular policy, higher education scholars say they need to decide on a unified message they want to convey about higher ed—something they’ve struggled to do in recent years.

Brendan Cantwell, a professor in the Higher, Adult, and Lifelong Education program at Michigan State University, says at least on the academic front, the message must be deeper than making college affordable and easier to deliver than making college free.

“It can lead to disillusionment when you promise that you’re going to deliver free college, but then are unable to deliver anything close to what an ordinary person believes is free,” Cantwell said, noting that free college and universal loan forgiveness were at the crux of Biden’s campaign and neither came to be at the federal level. “That’s why a more fruitful approach for Democrats might be to think about articulating a vision for society that includes higher education and then go for policies that flow from that.”

When Democrats last controlled Congress and the White House in 2021 and 2022, they doled out billions to colleges and universities for COVID-19 relief and boosted research with the CHIPS and Science Act. They also closed the 90/10 loophole to protect student veterans from predatory for-profit institutions and expanded the Pell grant accessible to incarcerated students. However, they failed to deliver on the party’s progressive promise to provide some debt relief.

A unified vision for the purpose of higher education, however, could set the Democrats up for future success.

“It’s about coming up with a compelling vision that ties to broader concerns about housing and transportation and helps people understand Democrats have a concrete plan to create a kind of life that people see as inviting and promising, the sort of future people want,” Cantwell said.

After two years, Dominique Baker, an associate professor of education and public policy at the University of Delaware, hopes she’ll be able to walk up to “any given Democrat in D.C.” and ask “What is the purpose of higher education?” and get a similar response. Like Cantwell, Baker hopes it’s more than just helping people get jobs.

“That, to me, misses the power and responsibility of the U.S. higher education system,” she said.

Use Oversight as a Tool

One of the best ways Democrats can convey their message and frame discussions about higher ed is through hearings and investigations that highlight how the Trump administration’s actions—including dismantling the Education Department—have affected institutions and students.

For example, a hearing on how Education Secretary Linda McMahon used interagency agreements to dismantle her department without Congressional approval could more specifically spotlight how moving the Office for Civil Rights to the Department of Justice has led to a backlog of unprocessed complaints.

“Conversations about civil rights investigations, which do not appear to be happening, can be tied to things like the Cornell incident,” Baker said, referring to a sexual assault complaint filed by a former student at Cornell University which alleged she had been gang raped by seven fraternity brothers at the Ivy-League institution.

But higher ed advocates and observers hope the Democrats go beyond questioning Trump officials about what’s not working and also spotlight the leaders of community colleges and regional public universities where earning a degree is affordable and job placement rates are high. Congress should also talk to everyday citizens to hear what issues matter most, experts add.

“One of the rarest things we get on hearing panels is a token person that represents students’ or parents’ thoughts,” Baker said. “Realistically, having field hearings that aren’t in D.C. are incredibly important, both from a messaging standpoint, but also for getting more information about how people are experiencing their education and where the cracks are happening?”

Loan Limits Reforms

Few of the experts Inside Higher Ed spoke with think the Democrats will be able to advance meaningful legislation that becomes law outside the annual must-pass spending bills. But the lawmakers can introduce and consider legislation that paves the way for future changes. Republicans made similar moves during 2023 and 2024 that led to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.

They hope Democrats will prioritize passing the College Transparency Act, which has been around for nearly a decade and would require the government to collect and share more data across agencies to track how students fare after they graduate. They also want lawmakers to standardize financial aid offers and create stronger support services for students working to exit loan default.

Those changes would support Democrats’ campaign promises of affordability and the broader message about colleges’ role in a healthy democracy, several experts argued.

What would not be a good idea, several experts including Akers and Domino said, is if Democrats spent their political capital over the next two years unsuccessfully trying to repeal the graduate loan limits and federal earnings test Trump backed in the Big Beautiful Bill. Several key House lawmakers ranked repealing them as one of their top priorities. Some university presidents and a graduate school dean told Inside Higher Ed they also preferred a clean repeal.

A number of financial aid policy experts, however, urged Congress to consider less costly compromises, such as changing which programs are eligible for the higher loan cap outlined in the law. One bipartisan bill was already proposed in 2026 to adjust the rules for the loan limits, so that idea could gain more traction.

The experts recommend lawmakers focus on designating critical health care careers like nursing, speech pathology and physician’s assistants as professional, which makes their students eligible for the higher loan limit of $50,000 a year. Another option would be adjusting what the cap is and raising it for careers like medicine and law that are proven to have a strong return on investment, and establishing grants for high-demand low-pay careers like teaching and social work.

“A blanket repeal isn’t going to pass in this administration,” Holt said. “But I really do hope that the parties can work together because I find this to be an unstable and unsustainable situation for borrowers who are trying to figure out how to go to school right now.”

Alex Ricci, president of the National Council of Higher Education Resources, a trade group focused on higher ed finance, added that “there's only so much money to go around.”

So while it’s fine to identify a lengthy wishlist, in the end it could come down to whether Democrats would rather double the Pell grant or lift the loan limit.

“You have to pick and choose,” he said.

title: How Young Voters Fueled Democratic Victories
summary:
How Young Voters Fueled Democratic Victories
Joshua.Bay Fri, 11/06/2026 - 03:00 AM

New data from Tufts University reveals how voters aged 18 to 29 shaped the 2026 midterms, driven by economic concerns and shifting political loyalties.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
A variety of issues motivated young voters to head to the polls in the 2026 midterm elections, ranging from the economy and jobs to health care and the war in Iran. Their participation helped fuel historic levels of support for Democratic candidates, contributing to the party’s victories that shifted control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.

New data from the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University found that nationally, 66 percent of young voters ages 18 to 29 supported Democratic candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives, compared to 31 percent who supported Republicans. In several key states, the researchers found, young voters played a significant role in Democratic victories.

Leela Strong, the Newhouse executive director at CIRCLE, said during a post-election briefing Thursday that young men, rural youth and young people without a college degree—groups that were consequential to President Trump's victory in 2024—were among those who shifted their support toward Democrats this year. She argued that the swing demonstrates how young voters, particularly Gen Z, are not necessarily driven by party loyalty or a single issue, but rather by a range of concerns.

“Young people, we know from all of our research, are not transactional voters,” Strong said. “They are acting on concerns about the economy and a democracy that isn’t working for their generation, and rewarding candidates who hear and see them.”

Youth voter patterns: The 35-point margin of support for Democrats among young voters in 2026 is one of the largest recorded in a national election, according to the report, which drew on data from The Voter Poll by SSRS and population estimates calculated by CIRCLE. It also marks a return to the strong Democratic support seen among young voters in election cycles before 2024.

Strong noted that early estimates show that roughly 27 percent of eligible young voters ages 18 to 29 cast a ballot in the 2026 midterms. That is within a few percentage points of the highest youth turnout rate for a midterm election in American history, she said. For decades, midterm youth turnout hovered around 20 percent before reaching a high of 31 percent in 2018 and 27 percent in 2022.

“Being in that range again matters,” Strong said. “It tells us that young people are sending a clear signal that they want to take action and drive change, and that this is no longer just an anomaly around a single election.”

“This number is consequential given that midterm electorates are smaller and older than presidential cycles,” she added. “It does not mean that youth decide every race. It means they cannot be treated as marginal in a tight one.”

Young voters’ support for Democratic candidates contrasts sharply with the voting patterns of other age groups, particularly those over 45. While 65 percent of young voters and 56 percent of those between 30 and 44 supported a Democratic House candidate, Americans over age 45 split their votes more evenly. Among voters ages 45 to 64, 51 percent supported Democrats and 46 percent supported Republicans, compared to 52 percent and 46 percent, respectively, among voters 65 and older.

“Young people represented about 11 percent of the electorate on Tuesday, and in close races, that kind of consistent block can affect the outcome,” Strong said. “This is what it looks like when young people are heard and seen in places where it counts.”

“Young people have impact—not just because they show up in large numbers, not just because they vote decisively in a different direction, but often because they vote very differently than older voters,” Alberto Medina, communications manager at CIRCLE, said during the briefing.

The report found that young women and young people of color were more likely to support Democratic candidates. Unlike in 2024, however, white youth and young men also showed strong support for Democrats, contributing to the party’s overwhelming advantage among young voters.

A notable gender gap remains in the youth vote. Some 70 percent of young women voted for a Democratic U.S. House candidate in the 2026 midterms, compared to 59 percent of young men. That represents a significant shift from 2024, the report notes, when 56 percent of young men supported President Trump.

An even larger difference emerged based on sexual orientation. Among young voters who identified as LGBTQ+, 86 percent supported a Democratic House candidate. By comparison, 57 percent of straight youth voted Democratic and 39 percent voted Republican.

“When we’re talking about the youth vote, it’s very important to not treat it as a monolith and pay attention to some of these demographic differences,” Medina said. “These differences are crucial to understand … because in a year when most demographics voted for Democratic candidates, it can range from 54 percent for a young white man to 86 percent for a young black woman.”

Medina also highlighted the shift among young Latino men, who were nearly evenly divided in 2024, with a slight preference for President Trump. In 2026, roughly two-thirds supported Democratic House candidates.

Educational attainment was another important factor this election, Medina said. Young people without college experience, including those whose highest level of education was a high school diploma or less, also supported Democratic candidates by significant margins. Among young college graduates, 70 percent voted for Democratic House candidates, compared to 28 percent who supported Republicans. Among those with a high school education or less, 60 percent supported Democrats and 35 percent supported Republicans.

“Non-college youth, like young white men, really turned out for Democrats in a way that we hadn’t seen at least in recent cycles,” Medina said.

Key issues: Medina said the economy was the top issue for young voters in the 2026 midterm elections. Some 52 percent selected the economy and jobs as one of the three most important issues facing the country.

Health care, another issue with significant economic implications, ranked second at 42 percent, followed by the war in Iran (27 percent), immigration (26 percent), education (21 percent) and climate change (20 percent).

Young people’s electoral choices also correlated with their top issues of concern. Those who selected climate change, racism and health care were the most likely to support a Democratic House candidate in the 2026 midterms.

Meanwhile, young voters who prioritized crime, immigration and the national debt were the most likely to support Republican candidates compared to those who selected other issues. Those who identified crime as a top concern were the only issue-based group in which a majority voted Republican, the CIRCLE report notes.

For many young voters, economic concerns reflected their own financial circumstances. Some 29 percent said they were “falling behind” economically, while 55 percent reported “holding steady.” Only 15 percent said they were “getting ahead.”

Voting preferences also differed based on young people’s financial circumstances. Those who reported getting ahead were relatively evenly divided, with 52 percent supporting Democratic House candidates and 46 percent supporting Republicans. By comparison, 65 percent of young voters who said they were holding steady and 73 percent of those falling behind voted for a Democratic House candidate.

“The economy is incredibly central to how they’re experiencing politics and what they want to see from politics,” Medina said. “So many of them say that they’re struggling, and as we can see in the data, the vast majority of young people who believe that they’re falling behind economically chose a Democratic candidate.”

Looking ahead: For Medina, Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race, which remained too close to call Thursday, illustrates the potential impact of young voters on election outcomes in a state that has long favored Republicans.

He noted during the briefing that 76 percent of Mississippi voters ages 18 to 29 supported the Democratic candidate, compared to 23 percent who supported the Republican. Among voters over 30, Democrats received 46 percent of the vote, compared to 51 percent for Republicans.

“There is dissatisfaction with the way things are going in the country, and for many young people, that’s not causing them to tune out of politics or to become completely disaffected,” Medina said. “For many, it’s causing them to lean in and believe that they can change that if they participate.”

Strong said CIRCLE’s forthcoming research will examine voting patterns among college students, trade and vocational school students, and young people without college experience.

“What we’re seeing is issues and candidates who are speaking to the broader concerns of this generation, and in doing so, they are eliciting the support for those candidates and those issues,” Strong said. “It is not about whether they are voting for a Democrat or voting for a Republican. They are more specifically voting for candidates and issues where they feel like they can see change over time.”

title: Net College Tuition Prices Keep Falling
summary:
Net College Tuition Prices Keep Falling
kathryn.palmer… Fri, 11/06/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
Adjusted for inflation, tuition and fees are getting cheaper at public colleges and universities, according to the Trends in College Pricing and Student Aid 2026 report the College Board published Thursday.

Between the 2016–17 and 2026–27 academic years, the average inflation-adjusted tuition and fees for in-district students declined by 12 percent at public colleges and 8 percent for in-state students attending public four-year universities. Meanwhile, tuition and fees remained flat at private nonprofit colleges. According to the report, the average sticker price for public four-year colleges this academic year was $12,290 for in-state students and $32,730 for out-of-state students. For students attending private, nonprofit colleges the average was $46,350.

However, many students receive grants, scholarships and other forms of aid that allow them to pay much less than the published sticker price.

“About 70 percent of full-time undergraduate students receive grant aid that reduces the actual cost of attending college,” Jessica Howell, College Board’s vice president of research, said in a news release. “Families need clear net price information early in the college application process.”

After adjusting for inflation, first-time full-time in-state students enrolled in public four-year institutions paid an estimated average of $1,920 in net tuition and fees during the 2026–27 academic year—compared to a peak of $4,600 during the 2012–13 academic year. Private college students have also seen a drop in average net tuition and fees over the past decade, from $20,350 (in 2026 value) during the 2016–17 academic year to $17,280 this academic year.

And at community colleges, the average first-time, full-time in-district students has been receiving enough grant aid to cover their tuition and fees since 2009.

But tuition and fees aren’t the only costs college students have to account for.

According to the report, during the 2026–27 academic year, community college students need $9,700 in housing and food after grant aid, in addition to $6,530 in allowances for books and supplies, transportation and other personal expenses. Students at public four-year colleges need about $16,350 for tuition, fees, housing and food after grant aid, and another $5,310 for personal expenses. And after grant aid, students at private colleges are still on the hook for an average of $38,540.

title: We need to talk about Meta: Political interference and interests in the Brazilian elections
summary: The company’s actions show that, above users’ rights, public interest, and democracy itself, prevails its economic interests and the maximization of their profits
full_text:
On the eve of Donald Trump’s return to the presidency of the United States, in January 2025, Meta’s founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that changes would be made to his company’s moderation policies in the name of “freedom of expression”, which, he said, was under threat by global pressures for what he saw as censorship. The announcement signaled a rapprochement between Meta and the far right around a common goal: the deregulation of Big Tech. Since then, growing entanglement between major technology companies and the U.S. President Donald Trump administration has shown how the private interests of a small group can override the public interest.

In recent months, allegations have been mounting that Big Tech companies, especially Meta, have been interfering in the Brazilian electoral process this year, aiming to undermine the reelection of President Lula (PT). This kind of accusation is not new. Over the past decade, a vast body of literature has exposed the mediating role played by digital platforms in foreign interference in elections around the world. These reports have also highlight the challenges of holding companies accountable for allowing these interference campaigns to be amplified.

At our research group, NetLab UFRJ, we have spent years investigating how major digital platforms shape public debate and influence people’s perceptions of reality, often outside the regulatory and normative frameworks in force in Brazil. Meta in particular has become fertile ground for disinformation and boosting fraudulent ads, which already account for 10% of its annual revenue.

Despite lawsuits and administrative actions brought by Brazilian authorities against Meta, complaints and requests from civil society for investigations, as well as reports published by the press, the company has shown neither the willingness nor the diligence needed to effectively fight this kind of content.

Given this troubling track record, NetLab UFRJ created the “Big Tech Observatory” during the 2026 election campaign period in order to monitor how Meta and other digital platforms performed in two key areas: algorithmic recommendation and political advertising. The initiative set out to examine whether these companies would comply with the current Brazilian legislation established by the Electoral Supreme Court (TSE). The results of the analyses, however, told a predictable story.

We found that, between July and September, Meta received approximately R$ 2 million (US$ 400,000) for running 1,613 ads placed from outside Brazil that aimed to either favor or harm candidates. All were paid for in foreign currencies and boosted by pages with declared locations in other countries. The amount invested in this advertising is equivalent to that spent on prominent campaigns, including the race for Presidency and other executive offices.

Brazilian electoral law expressly prohibits candidates from receiving cash or donations in-kind from abroad. This ban, however, did not prevent the ads from being displayed to Brazilian users of Meta’s platforms. According to the available information, not only the ads were allowed to circulate but they may have reached up to 171 million views in the country.

But the irregularities in advertising do not stop there. Brazilian electoral rules prohibit electoral advertising from 48 hours before the polls to 24 hours afterwards. However, our analyses of both rounds of the 2026 election identified hundreds of ads in favor or against specific candidates that circulated on Meta’s platforms with no apparent restrictions. The company even allowed fake profiles posing as official channels of the Electoral Supreme Court to boost disinformation about a supposed “digital vote” which stated that people would be allowed to cast their vote from home on the day of the first round — something which does not exist in the Brazilian electoral system.

In addition to these irregularities, Lula’s political campaign page was temporarily disabled by Meta without explanation, preventing it from running electoral ads. On September 23, his Worker´s Party (PT) reported they had been blocked from advertising on Meta’s platforms. In a statement released on October 16, the company rejected the accusations of election interference and attributed the temporary deactivation to an “incorrect anti-fraud review” carried out under an agreement with the federal government to fight fraud involving public programs.

The effectiveness of the company’s anti-fraud measures, however, is questionable: an analysis carried out by NetLab UFRJ identified hundreds of fraudulent ads involving federal public policies circulating before and after September 23, indicating that those same measures were not able to stop this kind of content from running during the same period.

Finally, we found signs of discriminatory practices in ad pricing. Based on data released by Meta, we estimate that for the first round Lula’s campaign may have paid between 33% and 43% more than his far right adversary Flávio Bolsonaro campaign to reach the same number of users on Meta’s platforms. Despite this substantial difference, limitations in the company’s transparency policies make it impossible to identify precisely which parameters and criteria are used to price ads and, consequently, to draw definitive conclusions about the mechanisms behind this disparity. Even so, studies conducted in other contexts, such as the United States, India and the Netherlands, also point to evidence of discriminatory pricing practices in the platform’s advertising.

Other complaints made during the elections add to this overall scenario of negligence and show that, despite being worth billions and their strategic position at the forefront of technological innovation, major digital platforms invest little in protecting their users. For example, this 2026 election in Brazil saw several controversies involving WhatsApp’s image generation service, powered by the Meta AI artificial intelligence. Users reported being able to generate content favorable to Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign without difficulty, whereas they were not getting the same results for Lula. Meanwhile, the documentary channel Revelando had videos criticizing Flávio Bolsonaro removed from its Instagram profiles shortly after they were posted, without clear justification from the company.

These episodes cast doubt on the consistency of Meta’s moderation and content control systems, exposing failures that call for greater investment and improvement. The situation is made worse by the absence of transparent criteria or guarantees of equal treatment in how ads are handled, how content is recommended, how advertising is priced, and how profiles and posts are moderated.

Big Tech companies have developed predatory business models, and they are currently joining forces with political forces committed to deregulation in Brazil. This is part of a strategy to protect their businesses and expand their room for maneuver.

Whether or not one side of the electoral race is being deliberately favored, it is indisputable that the major digital platforms continuously exercise the power to determine what gains visibility and what remains on the margins, with no transparency over their criteria and no mechanism for accountability. What is clear is that, for these platforms, defending their economic interests and maximizing their profits prevails above user rights, public interest, and democracy itself.

title: King Arthur and Ramayana: ancient stories that speak to the moral dilemmas of today’s leaders
summary: Although separated by centuries, these two epics pose dilemmas that separate the morality of the husband from the duty of the leader.
full_text:
Across the vastly different worlds of ancient India and medieval Britain, two legendary rulers face the exact same impossible choice: sacrifice their love or shatter the moral foundation of their kingdom? It feels strikingly familiar in an era where modern heads of state are still forced to choose between personal loyalty and institutional justice.

The ancient Hindu epic Ramayana (attributed to Valmiki, 750-500BC) tells the story of Rama, prince and eventual king of Ayodhya, and his struggle to rescue his wife Sita after she is abducted by the demon-king Ravana. More than two millennia later, T.H. White’s The Once and Future King (1958) retells the Arthurian legend, his round table and the tragic love triangle between him, his queen, Guenever and the greatest knight of his realm, Lancelot.

Although separated by centuries, these two epics arrive at the same disturbing question: should the king let his queen burn? It is a dilemma that separates the morality of the husband from the duty of the leader.

This article is part of Rethinking the Classics. The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

After rescuing Sita and slaying Ravana, Rama initially rejects his wife. However privately certain he is of Sita’s loyalty, as a king, he must reckon with the public morality of his realm. Is a woman who has lived in another man’s captivity fit to be the queen? Furious, Sita demands a test by fire herself. She pleads with the god of fire not to let her burn if she has remained faithful to her husband and walks into the flames unscathed.

Queen Guenever, on the other hand, really is unfaithful to Arthur. As a husband, he has long made peace with her and Lancelot’s relationship, as he loves them both dearly. But when the other knights of Arthur’s court catch them red-handed in adultery, Arthur can no longer look away. As king, he is duty bound to submit to and uphold the public morality of his kingdom. He orders that Guenever be burnt at the stake. What makes the dilemma even greater for both kings is that both are bringers of a moral code to their respective realms.

Arthur dedicates his entire reign to implement his extraordinary political experiment of replacing “might” with “right”. He replaces brute force with a system of justice that binds even him. To this end, he creates his famous Round Table, recruiting knights who use their valour and strength to help the weak, thus transforming power from an instrument of oppression into that of law and order.

Rama too, is a great political innovator. Upon his ascension to the throne, he establishes Ram-Rajya – a utopian state of righteousness and equality before law.

When faced with the impossible choice between breaking moral codes or letting their queens burn, they decide to uphold the morality of their kingdoms at great personal cost.

It is of little consequence that Lancelot rescues Guenever and that fire itself refuses to burn Sita. Both kings must endure terrible suffering for their choice. T.H White’s Arthur laments:

What is right? […] What is wrong? If Lancelot does come to rescue her, he may kill those innocent fellows of the guard, which I have sent to burn her. They have trusted me and I have put them there to keep him off, because it is justice. If he saves her, they will be killed. If they are not killed, she will be burned. But burned to death, […], in horrible burning flames – and she is my much-loved Gwen.

Valmiki’s Rama is forced by the god of fire to justify himself not just to Sita but to the three worlds of the heavens, the earth and the netherworld. He pleads:

Before the three worlds, Sita needed to be purified. She had dwelt for a long period time in Ravana’s inner quarters. Had she not been purified, virtuous people would have told me that I am foolish and driven by desire. I know that Sita is single-mindedly devoted to me and that her mind is only on me. However, I am devoted to the truth.

Ultimately, Arthur’s “right” would have burnt Guenever alive were it not for the “might” of Lancelot. And it is precisely Rama’s Ram-Rajya that leads to the unfair treatment of Sita.

In both epics, paradoxically, good triumphs only when the prevailing moral order or justice system is defied. It is this inherent and underlying contradiction within both texts that makes them resonate with many of our very contemporary concerns.

When might makes right

When Joe Biden granted an “unconditional” presidential pardon to his son Hunter Biden for tax and gun-related offences in 2024, critics accused him of abusing public power to protect his own family.

Weeks later, on his first day back in office, Donald Trump granted sweeping clemency to nearly 1,600 people charged with or convicted of offences stemming from the January 6 Capitol attack.

The circumstances might be different, but the dilemma is very much the same that we find in Valmiki and T.H White’s texts: do our leaders have the right to a private morality?

It is their capacity to ask such profound and enduring questions that has kept both the Ramayana and the legend of King Arthur alive across centuries. Both stories have and will be retold by each generation and will continue to return as novels, films, TV series and graphic novels.

For anyone wishing to enter these wonderful worlds, my recommendation would be to begin with T. H. White’s The Once and Future King and Valmiki’s Ramayana, available in an excellent English translation by Bibek Debroy. Read together, they show why the epics still matter. They don’t give us easy answers, but they teach us how to ask better questions.

Beyond the canon

As part of the Rethinking the Classics series, we’re asking our experts to recommend a book or artwork that tackles similar themes to the canonical work in question, but isn’t (yet) considered a classic itself. Here is Harsh Trivedi’s suggestion:

May Our Joy Endure by Laura-Ève Lambert (2022) explores the moral contradictions of power through the character of Céline Wachowski.

Wachowski is a celebrated architect based in Montreal who gets “cancelled” following an exposé on the malpractices of her architectural firm. The novel explores a complex dilemma: can someone be both responsible for injustice and a victim of it?

Like Rama and Arthur, Wachowski finds herself caught between her personal convictions and the judgment of others. But unlike the two kings, who sacrifice their personal happiness in the name of public morality, Wachowski attempts to use her privilege to define what is right and influence the public narrative in her favour.

This article features references to books that have been included for editorial reasons, and may contain links to bookshop.org. If you click on one of the links and go on to buy something, The Conversation UK may earn a commission.

title: The ‘unpoliceability’ of AI journal policies
summary: by Dirk Lindebaum Core to the mission of SRHE is the commitment to high-quality research and scholarship to advance understanding of higher education. This focus makes the conditions under which research is produced, including editorial and journal policies concerning the … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Dirk Lindebaum

Core to the mission of SRHE is the commitment to high-quality research and scholarship to advance understanding of higher education. This focus makes the conditions under which research is produced, including editorial and journal policies concerning the publication process, a topic of natural interest to readers of the SRHE blog.

The publication process, and how stakeholders interact in that process, however, is profoundly changing due to the widespread use of generative AI (hereafter AI). Consider the irony that authors can now offload their writing to AI; that reviewers can use AI to perform reviews on AI-produced text; and that editors can use AI to make decisions on papers written by AI, and grounding decisions in AI-produced reviews. It is machines chatting with machines, and machines reacting to machines, just without the informed doubt, the willingness of daring to know, the realization that we as social scientists always condition and are conditioned through our work and social practices that follow from our work.

Notwithstanding this development, the use of AI in the research process is routinely and boldly argued to be ‘inevitable’. What is less often understood is that this narrative likely accelerates an already existing crisis of credibility in some fields (eg in management research). A sobering look at the available empirical evidence (summarized here) underlines that the crisis is real.

First, empirical studies suggest that, in 2025, more than 140,000 non-existing references have infiltrated scientific records. Second, while the quality of scholarship is decreasing (as indicated through a measure of language complexity), the use of AI helps researchers to produce more papers and faster (with direct effects on individual careers). All this unfolds against an already disadvantageous baseline, where disruptive and innovate research occurs less often. Third, while many AI journal polices exhort scholars to be the ‘human-in-the-loop’ to check the accuracy of AI outputs, empirical studies suggest that AI biases (caused by human biases in the training data) transfer and magnify in humans through epistemic feedback loops in Human-AI interactions. Fourth, many authors neglect to disclose AI-use, the consequence being that many AI journal policies fail to ensure transparency or constrain AI adoption. Hence, many AI journal policies concerning the use of AI may attempt to ‘police the unpoliceable’, despite the well-intending motives behind such policies.

After years of editorial frontline experience, I believe two policy moves are necessary to counter these developments which, if unaddressed, likely compromise the integrity of science. On the one hand, qualitatively speaking, I propose a set of evaluative criteria concerning how to evaluate (as editors and reviewers), and prepare submissions (as authors), in ways that mobilise judgment to strengthen the voice of authors in terms of mastery of the literature, method, analysis, contribution and recommendations for practice. Developing editor and reviewer judgment to strengthen author voices, and for authors to force themselves to nurture said judgment to inform their own voices distinctly and uniquely, is a matter of paramount importance when the defining scarcity of our time is not access to information or even knowledge, but rather the capacity to develop and apply sound judgment in the presence of seemingly boundless AI slop. I treat judgment here as epistemic judgment concerning reflexive justifications for truth claims – to oneself and others under conditions of uncertainty – and as expressed through the authors’ voice.

This effort has to be earned. This means persisting with developing judgment over time, not despite the struggle involved, but because of it. This is exactly why this struggle matters for AI advocates. While some argue that one needs to be an expert to use the AI in research, this point is often based on decades of building expertise before the arrival of AI. Yet, current socialization practices are such that junior colleagues and PhD students may not find the conditions in which to develop expertise. This does and will negatively affect expertise levels now and in future. The result is that the conditions of re-building expertise shrink, and that means the possibility to recover lost expertise decreases. It seems to me a caution that needs to be put plainly – this should concern usall. However, these ‘qualitative’ criteria are unworkable without also creating the conditions in which editors and reviewers can manage the current deluge of journal submissions.

Therefore, the second, quantitative, proposal is to introduce a submission cap per authors per annum (as assessed by ORCID IDs), given record numbers of submissions to many journals across science subjects. This would provide necessary ‘breathing space’ for often overstretched (volunteering) editors and reviewers, while promoting equitable access to editorial resources, reduce congestion in the peer review pipeline, and discourage the use of the journal as a preliminary check on manuscript submission readiness. Lastly, a submission cap can also counter the creeping ‘junkification’ of science – the mounting volume of low-quality content that permeate academic publishing, which will only intensify in the age of Gen-AI.

Subject to amendments to suit the needs of a particular journal, the proposal would work like this: each author can submit three new submissions per year to a journal, but with a twist to encourage authors to improve the quality of first submission. For each invitation to revise and resubmit a paper, authors could submit one additional paper to a journal (3 + 1). And if they are lucky to get a second (or third) invitation to revise and resubmit a paper, then that number would be 3 + 2 etc. The expansion is author-specific; if submission A gets a revise and resubmit, every author listed on submission A receives +1 to their personal limit at this journal. This expansion would apply to new submissions, and not to invited revisions.

Some colleagues may have reservations about the proposal due to a perceived limit to their productivity. However, let’s appreciate that even if a prolific scholar manages to publish three articles in each of the best five journals in their fields per year, these 15 articles can hardly be said to be detrimental to the scholar’s career prospects.

A submission cap is consistent with scientific progress because it helps editors and reviewers regain vital space to write quality letters and reviews based on the proposed new set of evaluative criteria. Hence, it is key to consider the complementary nature of both proposals, with the benefit of enabling the conditions under which published works can be trusted (more) in the age of Gen-AI. Epistemic agency would flow back to journals and their editors, for academics would set the agenda (rather than big tech).

Rather than advocating contra AI in the research process, my stance here is pro developing human judgment. If developed and assessed well in the research process, the focus on judgment will render the debate around AI journal policies of secondary relevance. Why try to police the unpoliceable if investing in human judgment is one of the best ways to safeguard the integrity of science?

Dirk Lindebaum is Professor of Management & Organisation at the University of Bath, and advocate and owner of “AI-Free Scholarship” which is a registered (noncommercial) trademark that applies to his writing and teaching.

title: Protests and reforms: France's rising debt costs threaten stability
summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?
full_text:
Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

A barometer of France's public finances

The spread acts as a kind of fever gauge for bond markets, explains Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide towards a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he explained.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fuelled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE (the French national statistics agency — the ed.), 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

Echoes of the eurozone crisis

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

A warning shot for Germany

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warns the Mannheim-based economist.

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left La France insoumise (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire." "Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he claims.

'Fairy tales from the left and the right'

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales." Their common message, he says, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," the expert points out.

"In the past, currency devaluations (of the French franc — the ed.) made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This piece was originally published in German.

title: Young Factor Europe, sei Paesi a lezione di finanza
summary: Capire l’economia e la finanza per scegliere il futuro. Young Factor Europe porta l’educazione economico-finanziaria nelle scuole superiori di sei Paesi, con una piattaforma gratuita e un percorso costruito su...
full_text:
Capire l’economia e la finanza per scegliere il futuro. Young Factor Europe porta l’educazione economico-finanziaria nelle scuole superiori di sei Paesi, con una piattaforma gratuita e un percorso costruito su 50 parole chiave. Andrea Ceccherini, fondatore e presidente di Osservatorio for Independent Thinking, ha presentato la nuova edizione a Milano davanti alla presidente Bce Christine Lagarde e a 600 studenti.

Ceccherini: «Esercizio per partecipare alla vita democratica»

La posta in gioco supera la gestione dei risparmi: «Studiare la finanza e l’economia – spiega Ceccherini – è oggi un esercizio per partecipare a pieno titolo alla democrazia». Quello dell’alfabetizzazione economico-finanziaria,ha commentato la governatrice della Bce, è «un tema che mi sta particolarmente a cuore e che considero una componente essenziale della libertà: in particolare per le donne, conoscere gli strumenti finanziari e disporre delle competenze necessarie per gestire le proprie risorse significa poter compiere scelte autonome e decidere del proprio futuro». Da qui il «ringraziamento» all’Osservatorio per l’alto valore civile dell’iniziativa e «per il lavoro che sta facendo».

Loading...

Le Cinquanta parole

termini Il progetto è in fase pilota avanzata in Italia, Germania e Spagna e avviata in Francia, Paesi Bassi e Portogallo. Nel nostro Paese il progetto è sostenuto da Intesa Sanpaolo e UniCredit ai quali si aggiungerà anche Crédit Agricole Italia.

Il fulcro sono 50 parole, spiegate e illustrate, che si affrontano in cinque anni: test per misurare le conoscenze, videolezioni, attualità, masterclass dei governatori delle banche centrali e attività pratiche. A disposizione di docenti e studenti il giornalismo di Financial Times, The Economist, Wall Street Journal e Sole 24 Ore, attraverso la piattaforma Doubt and Debate.

Lagarde: «Questioni finanziarie ancora poco capite»

Quanto sia necessario questo alfabeto lo indica la stessa Lagarde parlando davanti agli studenti a Milano: in Europa, osserva, «il 50% dei cittadini ha una comprensione molto limitata delle questioni finanziarie. C’è chi fatica a distinguere un tasso fisso da uno variabile». Lacune che si riflettono sulla capacità di valutare un’offerta, gestire le proprie risorse e decidere con consapevolezza.

title: Big Tech sotto pressione: le mosse dei democratici dopo le midterm
summary:
Dopo la conquista di Camera e Senato alle elezioni americane, i democratici preparano audizioni dei vertici tecnologici, controlli sui modelli AI e regole sui data center. Le moratorie di Sanders, il FRONTIER Act bipartisan, la pressione delle comunità locali e i rischi per gli investimenti aprono una stagione di scontro con la Silicon Valley

L'articolo Big Tech sotto pressione: le mosse dei democratici dopo le midterm proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
Dopo mesi di deferenza verso Donald Trump, visite alla Casa Bianca e manifestazioni di fedeltà politica, per le Big Tech americane, che avevano cercato nell’asse con il presidente una sponda per i propri interessi, potrebbe profilarsi un brusco cambio di stagione.

La vittoria dei democratici alle elezioni di metà mandato del 3 novembre 2026 ha consegnato loro il controllo di Camera e Senato. Dal 3 gennaio 2027, con l’insediamento del nuovo Congresso, potranno guidare le commissioni, convocare i vertici delle aziende tecnologiche, pretendere documenti e mettere ai voti misure su intelligenza artificiale, data center, concorrenza e protezione dei minori.

L’offensiva è già cominciata sul piano politico. Greg Casar, deputato del Texas e presidente del Congressional Progressive Caucus, ha dichiarato: «I CEO delle aziende di AI dovrebbero essere chiamati a testimoniare sotto giuramento». Ed Markey, senatore del Massachusetts, ha evocato un’ondata di mandati di comparizione. Frank Pallone, esponente democratico di riferimento della commissione Energia e Commercio della Camera, ha indicato fra le priorità tutela dei consumatori, ambiente, energia pulita e contenimento del potere delle grandi piattaforme, come ha ricostruito.

Il contrasto con la Casa Bianca è già definito. Un ordine esecutivo di Donald Trump del giugno 2026 prevede verifiche volontarie sulle capacità cyber dei modelli AI di frontiera ed esclude che quelle misure autorizzino licenze obbligatorie per svilupparli o distribuirli. I democratici più interventisti vogliono invece un nuovo regolatore federale e perfino una pausa degli sviluppi avanzati. Per trasformare queste proposte in leggi dovranno confrontarsi con la Casa Bianca e cercare voti anche fuori dall’ala progressista.

Le iniziative sul tavolo hanno portata diversa: alcune sono proposte di sospensione dell’espansione industriale, altre disegnano regole di trasparenza e sicurezza. Ecco le principali, con il loro stato al 6 novembre 2026.

Le iniziative politiche e legislative sulle Big Tech

Fonti: ufficio Sanders (marzo 2026), testo H.R. 10538, ufficio Trahan, Commissione Commercio del Senato, Commissione Giustizia del Senato. Tutti i progetti di legge citati sono ancora proposte al 6 novembre 2026

Il voto ha trasformato l’ostilità verso i data center in forza politica

Una parte della svolta nasce lontano da Washington, nei comuni che devono autorizzare i grandi poli di calcolo e le infrastrutture per alimentarli. Prezzo dell’elettricità, consumo d’acqua, uso del territorio e benefici economici locali sono diventati argomenti elettorali. Il malcontento colpisce in particolare gli impianti destinati all’AI, il cui sviluppo richiede potenza elettrica e investimenti su scala crescente.

Nel riepilogo delle consultazioni locali del 2026 aggiornato al 4 novembre, Ballotpedia conta 46 esiti favorevoli a restrizioni su 47 misure decise: sono compresi sia i divieti approvati, sia i voti contrari a proposte che avrebbero facilitato nuovi insediamenti. L’unica eccezione è Harwood, nel North Dakota, dove gli elettori hanno bocciato nuovi obblighi di esame per alcuni sviluppi industriali. Sono risultati provvisori e comprendono anche referendum consultivi.

La dimensione concreta del fenomeno emerge da alcuni risultati: Alhambra, in California, ha approvato un divieto con l’82% dei voti; Edgewater, in Florida, con il 77%. A Bloomington, Illinois, il 78% ha sostenuto una moratoria consultiva sui grandi impianti. In molte altre località è stata respinta la possibilità di costruire nuovi data center oppure sono state approvate soglie massime di potenza e nuove autorizzazioni.

Anche le campagne elettorali hanno sfruttato questa opposizione. Il Tech Oversight Project, organizzazione impegnata a favore di maggiori controlli sul settore, ha esaminato messaggi pubblicitari di oltre 130 competizioni considerate rilevanti. L’accountability delle aziende tecnologiche compare nel 74% delle campagne democratiche «Red-to-Blue» per la Camera, nell’86% delle sfide per il Senato valutate in equilibrio e nel 100% delle gare per governatore classificate «toss-up». Le categorie sono selezionate e di dimensioni diverse: descrivono le campagne esaminate, non tutte le elezioni americane.

Sanders vuole fermare i nuovi impianti e rallentare l’AI avanzata

La risposta più radicale arriva da Bernie Sanders, senatore indipendente del Vermont che siede con i democratici. Subito dopo il voto ha rilanciato la richiesta di una moratoria nazionale sui nuovi data center per l’intelligenza artificiale. È una posizione che aveva già trasformato in una proposta legislativa insieme ad Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez il 25 marzo 2026, con l’AI Data Center Moratorium Act.

Il progetto prevede una sospensione degli insediamenti legati all’AI fino all’introduzione di salvaguardie federali: protezioni per lavoratori e diritti, limiti agli effetti sulle tariffe energetiche e sull’ambiente, benefici economici condivisi. Contiene anche restrizioni all’esportazione di infrastrutture di calcolo AI verso Paesi privi di tutele considerate sufficienti. Per i costruttori di grandi campus la posta in gioco è la possibilità stessa di avviare nuovi progetti, prima ancora del costo delle autorizzazioni.

Sanders ha promosso anche un secondo intervento, più ambizioso. Il Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, H.R. 10538, presentato alla Camera da Casar il 24 settembre, con Yassamin Ansari fra i cofirmatari, mira a vietare lo sviluppo della superintelligenza artificiale e a sospendere quello dei sistemi avanzati finché una nuova autorità federale non abbia stabilito regole e verifiche di sicurezza. La proposta crea un dipartimento dedicato all’AI, con poteri di controllo e sanzioni particolarmente severe.

Ansari, deputata democratica dell’Arizona, ha chiesto dopo le elezioni che la pausa nello sviluppo dell’AI avanzata e il divieto di superintelligenza entrino fra le priorità del nuovo Congresso. Casar ha sostenuto pubblicamente l’appello. Le due moratorie intervengono su oggetti differenti: la prima sulle infrastrutture di calcolo, la seconda sulle attività di sviluppo di determinati sistemi. Un eventuale accordo politico dovrebbe definire con precisione quali impianti e modelli siano interessati.

A poche ore dalla sua vittoria, in Texas, sul candidato Repubblicano Ken Paxton, James Talarico ha promesso di porre un freno all’espansione dei data center, eliminando le agevolazioni fiscali per chi li realizza, imponendo agli operatori di sostenere integralmente i propri costi energetici e introducendo forme di redistribuzione dei benefici economici dell’intelligenza artificiale a favore dei cittadini.

Dal FRONTIER Act alla tutela dei minori: la strada delle regole

Nel partito convivono anche posizioni più favorevoli alla continuazione dello sviluppo tecnologico, purché sottoposto a verifiche. Un esempio concreto è il FRONTIER Act, presentato il 23 luglio 2026 dalla democratica Lori Trahan e dal repubblicano Jay Obernolte insieme ad altri parlamentari dei due schieramenti. È un progetto che prova a costruire una cornice nazionale per i rischi dei modelli più avanzati, senza proporre una sospensione generalizzata della ricerca.

Secondo la presentazione ufficiale del FRONTIER Act, gli obblighi crescono in base alla dimensione dello sviluppatore: documentazione sui modelli, sistemi di gestione dei rischi, audit indipendenti, valutazioni continue e notifiche degli incidenti gravi. Per le imprese il cambiamento sarebbe soprattutto organizzativo: processi di valutazione verificabili, tracciamento degli eventi di sicurezza e informazioni da fornire a chi esercita la supervisione.

Su un altro versante il nuovo Congresso potrà riprendere le misure per bambini e adolescenti online. Il 5 agosto la Commissione Commercio del Senato ha fatto avanzare, fra le altre, il Kids Online Safety Act, lo Youth AI Privacy Act e il CHATBOT Act. Il dibattito riguarda progettazione dei servizi, raccolta dei dati dei minori e sicurezza delle interazioni con i chatbot: questioni che coinvolgono social network, app store e fornitori di AI conversazionale.

Il riassetto dei rapporti di forza può riaprire inoltre la partita sulla concorrenza digitale. L’American Innovation and Choice Online Act, rilanciato nel 2026 da Amy Klobuchar e Chuck Grassley, consentirebbe alle autorità antitrust di contestare condotte discriminatorie ed escludenti delle piattaforme dominanti che danneggiano la concorrenza. Qui il bersaglio principale sono le regole economiche con cui grandi ecosistemi digitali trattano concorrenti e imprese clienti.

Audizioni, contratti e rapporti con Trump: la leva più immediata

Le inchieste parlamentari potrebbero arrivare prima di qualsiasi legge. Il controllo delle commissioni permetterà ai democratici di chiedere documenti e testimonianze sull’influenza delle imprese tecnologiche sull’amministrazione Trump. Tra gli argomenti indicati nel dibattito figurano il ruolo di Elon Musk e del DOGE, i contratti federali, i rapporti fra governo e piattaforme e le conseguenze di scelte che hanno coinvolto servizi strategici come Starlink.

Questa leva ha effetti concreti sulle aziende: devono preparare dirigenti e documentazione, rispondere a richieste ufficiali, spiegare scelte commerciali e rapporti istituzionali. Le audizioni possono anche fornire elementi per proposte legislative successive. È il potere già acquisito con le elezioni, a differenza dei testi di legge, che richiedono maggioranze parlamentari sufficienti e la firma del presidente oppure i voti per superarne il veto.

Il compromesso resta cruciale. Le proposte depositate nell’attuale 119° Congresso dovranno essere ripresentate all’apertura del 120° Congresso, come indicano le regole del Senato. Inoltre, al Senato l’ostruzionismo può imporre una soglia di 60 voti per chiudere il dibattito su una legge ordinaria. Su moratorie e divieti radicali la distanza tra democratici moderati, progressisti e repubblicani è notevole; gli accordi bipartisan su audit, privacy e minori hanno una base politica diversa.

OpenAI cambia impegni sui data center, Anthropic teme per la Borsa

Le aziende stanno già adeguando il loro messaggio. Il 5 novembre OpenAI ha presentato il National Community Compact, con l’impegno a coprire integralmente il costo dell’elettricità e degli adeguamenti di rete, coinvolgere le comunità nei progetti, pubblicare dati su acqua ed energia e rendicontare i benefici occupazionali. Gli impegni annunciati riguardano i futuri campus che OpenAI possiederà e gestirà direttamente: una delimitazione importante, perché una parte delle capacità di calcolo viene realizzata da partner.

La stessa OpenAI ha chiesto regole pubbliche per dare alle comunità voce sulle autorizzazioni e sui costi degli impianti. È un segnale di come la discussione stia passando dagli annunci di investimento al problema di chi paga la rete, chi usa le risorse e chi decide se un progetto si realizza. Una stretta normativa può aumentare tempi e costi di costruzione, mentre la richiesta di maggiore trasparenza può rendere alcuni progetti più accettabili ai residenti.

Il clima si riflette anche sulla finanza dell’AI. Anthropic ha presentato il 26 ottobre il modulo S-1 per quotarsi al Nasdaq con il simbolo ANT e il 2 novembre ne ha depositato un aggiornamento alla Sec. Ma il 5 novembre Reuters ha riferito che alcuni potenziali investitori considerano ambiziosa la valutazione ipotizzata di circa 1.500 miliardi di dollari e sollevano dubbi sulla possibilità di mantenere il calendario dell’offerta, che prevedeva l’avvio del roadshow nella settimana del 9 novembre.

Dopo mesi di deferenza verso Donald Trump, visite alla Casa Bianca e manifestazioni di fedeltà politica, per le Big Tech americane, che avevano cercato nell’asse con il presidente una sponda per i propri interessi, potrebbe profilarsi un brusco cambio di stagione.

La vittoria dei democratici alle elezioni di metà mandato del 3 novembre 2026 ha consegnato loro il controllo di Camera e Senato. Dal 3 gennaio 2027, con l’insediamento del nuovo Congresso, potranno guidare le commissioni, convocare i vertici delle aziende tecnologiche, pretendere documenti e mettere ai voti misure su intelligenza artificiale, data center, concorrenza e protezione dei minori.

L’offensiva è già cominciata sul piano politico. Greg Casar, deputato del Texas e presidente del Congressional Progressive Caucus, ha dichiarato: «I CEO delle aziende di AI dovrebbero essere chiamati a testimoniare sotto giuramento». Ed Markey, senatore del Massachusetts, ha evocato un’ondata di mandati di comparizione. Frank Pallone, esponente democratico di riferimento della commissione Energia e Commercio della Camera, ha indicato fra le priorità tutela dei consumatori, ambiente, energia pulita e contenimento del potere delle grandi piattaforme, come ha ricostruito.

Il contrasto con la Casa Bianca è già definito. Un ordine esecutivo di Donald Trump del giugno 2026 prevede verifiche volontarie sulle capacità cyber dei modelli AI di frontiera ed esclude che quelle misure autorizzino licenze obbligatorie per svilupparli o distribuirli. I democratici più interventisti vogliono invece un nuovo regolatore federale e perfino una pausa degli sviluppi avanzati. Per trasformare queste proposte in leggi dovranno confrontarsi con la Casa Bianca e cercare voti anche fuori dall’ala progressista.

Le iniziative sul tavolo hanno portata diversa: alcune sono proposte di sospensione dell’espansione industriale, altre disegnano regole di trasparenza e sicurezza. Ecco le principali, con il loro stato al 6 novembre 2026.

Le iniziative politiche e legislative sulle Big Tech

Fonti: ufficio Sanders (marzo 2026), testo H.R. 10538, ufficio Trahan, Commissione Commercio del Senato, Commissione Giustizia del Senato. Tutti i progetti di legge citati sono ancora proposte al 6 novembre 2026

Il voto ha trasformato l’ostilità verso i data center in forza politica

Una parte della svolta nasce lontano da Washington, nei comuni che devono autorizzare i grandi poli di calcolo e le infrastrutture per alimentarli. Prezzo dell’elettricità, consumo d’acqua, uso del territorio e benefici economici locali sono diventati argomenti elettorali. Il malcontento colpisce in particolare gli impianti destinati all’AI, il cui sviluppo richiede potenza elettrica e investimenti su scala crescente.

Nel riepilogo delle consultazioni locali del 2026 aggiornato al 4 novembre, Ballotpedia conta 46 esiti favorevoli a restrizioni su 47 misure decise: sono compresi sia i divieti approvati, sia i voti contrari a proposte che avrebbero facilitato nuovi insediamenti. L’unica eccezione è Harwood, nel North Dakota, dove gli elettori hanno bocciato nuovi obblighi di esame per alcuni sviluppi industriali. Sono risultati provvisori e comprendono anche referendum consultivi.

La dimensione concreta del fenomeno emerge da alcuni risultati: Alhambra, in California, ha approvato un divieto con l’82% dei voti; Edgewater, in Florida, con il 77%. A Bloomington, Illinois, il 78% ha sostenuto una moratoria consultiva sui grandi impianti. In molte altre località è stata respinta la possibilità di costruire nuovi data center oppure sono state approvate soglie massime di potenza e nuove autorizzazioni.

Anche le campagne elettorali hanno sfruttato questa opposizione. Il Tech Oversight Project, organizzazione impegnata a favore di maggiori controlli sul settore, ha esaminato messaggi pubblicitari di oltre 130 competizioni considerate rilevanti. L’accountability delle aziende tecnologiche compare nel 74% delle campagne democratiche «Red-to-Blue» per la Camera, nell’86% delle sfide per il Senato valutate in equilibrio e nel 100% delle gare per governatore classificate «toss-up». Le categorie sono selezionate e di dimensioni diverse: descrivono le campagne esaminate, non tutte le elezioni americane.

Sanders vuole fermare i nuovi impianti e rallentare l’AI avanzata

La risposta più radicale arriva da Bernie Sanders, senatore indipendente del Vermont che siede con i democratici. Subito dopo il voto ha rilanciato la richiesta di una moratoria nazionale sui nuovi data center per l’intelligenza artificiale. È una posizione che aveva già trasformato in una proposta legislativa insieme ad Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez il 25 marzo 2026, con l’AI Data Center Moratorium Act.

Il progetto prevede una sospensione degli insediamenti legati all’AI fino all’introduzione di salvaguardie federali: protezioni per lavoratori e diritti, limiti agli effetti sulle tariffe energetiche e sull’ambiente, benefici economici condivisi. Contiene anche restrizioni all’esportazione di infrastrutture di calcolo AI verso Paesi privi di tutele considerate sufficienti. Per i costruttori di grandi campus la posta in gioco è la possibilità stessa di avviare nuovi progetti, prima ancora del costo delle autorizzazioni.

Sanders ha promosso anche un secondo intervento, più ambizioso. Il Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, H.R. 10538, presentato alla Camera da Casar il 24 settembre, con Yassamin Ansari fra i cofirmatari, mira a vietare lo sviluppo della superintelligenza artificiale e a sospendere quello dei sistemi avanzati finché una nuova autorità federale non abbia stabilito regole e verifiche di sicurezza. La proposta crea un dipartimento dedicato all’AI, con poteri di controllo e sanzioni particolarmente severe.

Ansari, deputata democratica dell’Arizona, ha chiesto dopo le elezioni che la pausa nello sviluppo dell’AI avanzata e il divieto di superintelligenza entrino fra le priorità del nuovo Congresso. Casar ha sostenuto pubblicamente l’appello. Le due moratorie intervengono su oggetti differenti: la prima sulle infrastrutture di calcolo, la seconda sulle attività di sviluppo di determinati sistemi. Un eventuale accordo politico dovrebbe definire con precisione quali impianti e modelli siano interessati.

A poche ore dalla sua vittoria, in Texas, sul candidato Repubblicano Ken Paxton, James Talarico ha promesso di porre un freno all’espansione dei data center, eliminando le agevolazioni fiscali per chi li realizza, imponendo agli operatori di sostenere integralmente i propri costi energetici e introducendo forme di redistribuzione dei benefici economici dell’intelligenza artificiale a favore dei cittadini.

Dal FRONTIER Act alla tutela dei minori: la strada delle regole

Nel partito convivono anche posizioni più favorevoli alla continuazione dello sviluppo tecnologico, purché sottoposto a verifiche. Un esempio concreto è il FRONTIER Act, presentato il 23 luglio 2026 dalla democratica Lori Trahan e dal repubblicano Jay Obernolte insieme ad altri parlamentari dei due schieramenti. È un progetto che prova a costruire una cornice nazionale per i rischi dei modelli più avanzati, senza proporre una sospensione generalizzata della ricerca.

Secondo la presentazione ufficiale del FRONTIER Act, gli obblighi crescono in base alla dimensione dello sviluppatore: documentazione sui modelli, sistemi di gestione dei rischi, audit indipendenti, valutazioni continue e notifiche degli incidenti gravi. Per le imprese il cambiamento sarebbe soprattutto organizzativo: processi di valutazione verificabili, tracciamento degli eventi di sicurezza e informazioni da fornire a chi esercita la supervisione.

Su un altro versante il nuovo Congresso potrà riprendere le misure per bambini e adolescenti online. Il 5 agosto la Commissione Commercio del Senato ha fatto avanzare, fra le altre, il Kids Online Safety Act, lo Youth AI Privacy Act e il CHATBOT Act. Il dibattito riguarda progettazione dei servizi, raccolta dei dati dei minori e sicurezza delle interazioni con i chatbot: questioni che coinvolgono social network, app store e fornitori di AI conversazionale.

Il riassetto dei rapporti di forza può riaprire inoltre la partita sulla concorrenza digitale. L’American Innovation and Choice Online Act, rilanciato nel 2026 da Amy Klobuchar e Chuck Grassley, consentirebbe alle autorità antitrust di contestare condotte discriminatorie ed escludenti delle piattaforme dominanti che danneggiano la concorrenza. Qui il bersaglio principale sono le regole economiche con cui grandi ecosistemi digitali trattano concorrenti e imprese clienti.

Audizioni, contratti e rapporti con Trump: la leva più immediata

Le inchieste parlamentari potrebbero arrivare prima di qualsiasi legge. Il controllo delle commissioni permetterà ai democratici di chiedere documenti e testimonianze sull’influenza delle imprese tecnologiche sull’amministrazione Trump. Tra gli argomenti indicati nel dibattito figurano il ruolo di Elon Musk e del DOGE, i contratti federali, i rapporti fra governo e piattaforme e le conseguenze di scelte che hanno coinvolto servizi strategici come Starlink.

Questa leva ha effetti concreti sulle aziende: devono preparare dirigenti e documentazione, rispondere a richieste ufficiali, spiegare scelte commerciali e rapporti istituzionali. Le audizioni possono anche fornire elementi per proposte legislative successive. È il potere già acquisito con le elezioni, a differenza dei testi di legge, che richiedono maggioranze parlamentari sufficienti e la firma del presidente oppure i voti per superarne il veto.

Il compromesso resta cruciale. Le proposte depositate nell’attuale 119° Congresso dovranno essere ripresentate all’apertura del 120° Congresso, come indicano le regole del Senato. Inoltre, al Senato l’ostruzionismo può imporre una soglia di 60 voti per chiudere il dibattito su una legge ordinaria. Su moratorie e divieti radicali la distanza tra democratici moderati, progressisti e repubblicani è notevole; gli accordi bipartisan su audit, privacy e minori hanno una base politica diversa.

Il 5 novembre OpenAI ha presentato il National Community Compact, con l’impegno a coprire integralmente il costo dell’elettricità e degli adeguamenti di rete, coinvolgere le comunità nei progetti, pubblicare dati su acqua ed energia e rendicontare i benefici occupazionali. Gli impegni annunciati riguardano i futuri campus che OpenAI possiederà e gestirà direttamente: una delimitazione importante, perché una parte delle capacità di calcolo viene realizzata da partner.

La stessa OpenAI ha chiesto regole pubbliche per dare alle comunità voce sulle autorizzazioni e sui costi degli impianti. È un segnale di come la discussione stia passando dagli annunci di investimento al problema di chi paga la rete, chi usa le risorse e chi decide se un progetto si realizza. Una stretta normativa può aumentare tempi e costi di costruzione, mentre la richiesta di maggiore trasparenza può rendere alcuni progetti più accettabili ai residenti.
